messages.author: 839dfa09184985a5
messages.subject: RNG for BetaBinom and ExpNormal
parts:
I've finished implementing RNG for all of the current distributions (except for ikj corr and cov). All of the RNG have passed the chi square goodness of fit test except for BetaBinomial and ExpoNormal (just finished adding this one today), as I do not know what to test these against--Boost Math does not have these distributions at all. Any ideas?

Also, for hypergeometric, I ended up implementing the RNG by using the cdf and returning the number of "successes" based on a uniform(0,1) random number (code below). I'll leave this for now, but does anyone have a better method?


Peter



template <class RNG>
inline int
hypergeometric_rng(int N,
int a,
int b,
RNG& rng) {
using boost::variate_generator;

boost::math::hypergeometric_distribution<>dist (b, N, a + b);
Eigen::VectorXd index(a);
for(int i = 0; i < a; i++)
index(i) = cdf(dist, i + 1);

double c = uniform_rng(0.0, 1.0, rng);
int d = 0;
while(c > index(d,0))
d++;
return d + 1;
}

parts:
There are some interesting methods in Numpy here:
https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/master/numpy/random/mtrand/distributions.c
though I can't speak to their effectiveness in practice.

At the very least you should consider a) using binary search instead
of linear, b) not bothering with the pregenerated table. Or c), if
you're going to be drawing many samples from the same hypergeo and the
range is reasonable, use the alias method, a really pretty and
poorly-known trick, explained at probably-too-much length here:
http://www.keithschwarz.com/darts-dice-coins/ and do all the
precomputation once.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] RNG for BetaBinom and ExpNormal
parts:
For the beta-binomial, you can generate variates
following the definition of the model:

generate y ~ beta_binomial(N,alpha,beta)

by

generate theta ~ beta(alpha,beta)

generate y ~ binomial(N,theta)

It's because the beta-binomial is defined as a compound
distribution as follows:

beta_binom(y|N,alpha,beta)

= INTEGEGRAL beta(theta|alpha,beta) binomial(y|N,theta) d.theta

The Wikipedia page needs some more work :-)

If ExpoNormal is a normal transform, you'll be able to do
the same kind of thing. Also, whatever it is, it needs to go
in the doc.

Having an inefficient hypergeometric's no big deal, at
least for now --- it's unlikely to find a lot of use.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: RNG for BetaBinom and ExpNormal
parts:
On Saturday, March 30, 2013 10:46:25 PM UTC-4, Peter Li wrote:
I've finished implementing RNG for all of the current distributions (except for ikj corr and cov).

I did the lkj_corr yesterday. A few general comments on your other RNGs:

-- I think the arguments should be const qualified wherever possible, like

poisson_rng(double lambda, ...
->
poisson_rng(const double lambda, ...

-- Eigen's .inverse() method should be avoided in Stan because it does not take advantage of positive definiteness. So, it is a bit slow and also does not rigorously preserve symmetry. I think the best construction is to use a Cholesky decomposition, as in

S.inverse()
->
S_inv = Eigen::MatrixXd::Identity(S.cols(),S.cols());
S_inv = S.ldlt().solve(S_inv); // no additional malloc

-- There is a multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose() function for multiplying a lower triangular matrix by its own transpose that takes into account symmetry and sparsity that you can use when necessary, like

S.llt().matrixL() * B * B.transpose() * S.llt().matrixL().transpose();
->
multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose(S.llt().matrixL() * B);

-- In wishart_rng, there is a

Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,Eigen::Dynamic> A(S.rows(), 1);

that is unused, and if it were used, it would be better to declare it as Eigen::VectorXd. Also, you can use the ::Zero(rows, cols) construction to allocate B with zeros rather than looping, see

http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox-devel/classEigen_1_1DenseBase.html#a724349af3e253b69a54d503931b52ec3

Otherwise it looks good. Thanks for doing all of these.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: foo(double) vs. foo(const double)?
parts:
On 4/4/13 11:50 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:

> -- I think the arguments should be const qualified wherever possible, like
>
> |
> poisson_rng(double lambda, ...
> ->
> poisson_rng(const double lambda, ...
> |

We haven't const qualified other double or int args
(or anything else passed by value) in the code.

Should we?

I was under the impression it didn't make much difference
because the const only scopes over the body of the
implementation --- that is, it doesn't change the interface
for a client of the API. Also, const is always just a
suggestion beause of const_cast.

Do any compilers make use of the const to help optimize?

- bob

> ->
> poisson_rng(const double lambda, ...
> |

We haven't const qualified other double or int args
(or anything else passed by value) in the code.

Should we?

I was under the impression it didn't make much difference
because the const only scopes over the body of the
implementation --- that is, it doesn't change the interface
for a client of the API.   Also, const is always just a
suggestion beause of const_cast.

Do any compilers make use of the const to help optimize?

I just do it because you can scan the signature to see what inputs are not going to be modified and to get a compiler error if the function accidentally modifies them. That is all without const_cast, but I think const_cast should not be used without having a comment at the top explaining it. For Eigen types, having the const serves another purpose in that the function can accept an expression thingie which it evaluates into a temporary. See

http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox-devel/TopicFunctionTakingEigenTypes.html

in the sections "In what cases do do functions taking plain Matrix or Array arguments {work, fail}?"

Ben

> Do any compilers make use of the const to help optimize?

> I just do it because you can scan the signature to see what inputs are not going to be modified

I agree for non-primitive arguments, but primitives behave
differently.

From a client perspective, foo(double) and foo(const double)
are identical. The const only controls whether you can reassign
the copy of the argument local to the function definition.

My inclination for primitive types is to follow the std lib,
which does NOT const qualify primitive arguments; e.g.,

http://www.cplusplus.com/reference/cmath/exp/

Another issue for the modification is that we should
be declaring member functions const wherever appropriate.
That is, something like:

double foo(double) const;

> and to get a compiler
> error if the function accidentally modifies them.
We'd get an error if we tried to modify the local copy.

> That is all without const_cast, but I think const_cast should not be
> used without having a comment at the top explaining it.

We haven't used it anywhere, and even if we const casted
a const double arg, it wouldn't change the behavior from
the client perspective.
> For Eigen types, having the const serves another purpose

We definitely don't want to pass these big structs by value
because that involves a lot of copying and allocation.

On the other hand, we return them by value, which can be
wasteful compared to passing in a non-const matrix reference
into which to write the results.

> in that
> the function can accept an expression thingie which it evaluates into a temporary. See
>
> http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox-devel/TopicFunctionTakingEigenTypes.html
>
> in the sections "In what cases do do functions taking plain Matrix or Array arguments {work, fail}?"

I still don't see how we can use this CRTP approach in our code
because of the strong distinction between row vectors,
column vectors and matrices.

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curiously_recurring_template_pattern

Maybe some kind of template magic could restrict application,
but I don't know there's much we can rely on in the Derived class.

- Bob
